title: p99/p95 tail latency deep dive with Spectra Labs
summary: Technical deep dive focused on Spectra's p95/p99 tail latency issues on Redwood hosted endpoints. Covered streaming vs non-streaming behavior, KV cache hit/miss patterns, batching settings, quantization tradeoffs, and network/topology causes (VPC peering, load balancer). Agreed on targeted benchmarks and follow-ups: share traces, run controlled A/B with and without KV cache, and attempt a quantized profile on dedicated nodes.

Topics: p95,p99 ; streaming vs non-streaming ; KV cache ; batching ; quantization ; VPC/network hops ; dedicated vs hosted

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: okay hi everyone, thanks for joining, um we thought we'd dive into the p95 p99 tail stuff you flagged, Maya's going to share some slides and traces, cool?
[00:18] Alex: yeah thanks Jordan, we have been seeing right, p95 around 110-130ms but p99 shooting up to 400-600ms on heavy days, that's what's killing our SLA for interactive product features.
[00:32] Maya: got it, thanks Alex. quick show of hands  you folks are on the hosted endpoint today, right? not dedicated?
[00:40] Sam: correct, hosted API in us-east-1 with VPC peering back to our infra for data pulls.
[00:48] Lina: and we do streaming for chat UI, non-streaming for some batch summarization.
[00:55] Maya: perfect. ok I'll pull up a trace  this first one is a p99 spike trace from last thursday, you'll see an initial TLS handshake / connection setup, then a KV cache miss, then the model comp takes longer, and finally a retry on the client side which makes it worse.
[01:18] Speaker 1: (screen) if you look at the timeline the big gap is between the request arrival at the load balancer and first token, there's about 320ms there on this sample.
[01:30] Alex: is that load balancer or gRPC proxy?
[01:33] Maya: in hosted flows there's a few pieces  LB, edge gateway, then the model host. if you have VPC peering there can be NAT and additional hops. in this trace we saw 80-120ms at the network layer sometimes.
[01:46] Sam: hmm we did some tests and saw a lot of short-lived connections; our infra creates a new socket per request sometimes.
[01:52] Jordan: yep, connection churn is a classic tail problem  TLS handshake cost, TCP slow start for small windows; keep-alive and connection pooling really help.
[02:04] Lina: we use HTTP/1.1 fetch in the client, is gRPC streaming better for tail?
[02:09] Maya: streaming can help hide compute variability because the server can send tokens as produced; for p99 if there's a big compute spike streaming will at least start returning tokens early. that said streaming also introduces jitter especially if tokenization or packaging latency is variable.
[02:26] Alex: so in our data streaming reduced p99 for interactive prompts by about 30% but for long responses p95 got noisier.
[02:36] Maya: that matches what we see. also KV cache  if you have a hot-prefix cache hit your latency is typically dominated by network hops + small model compute. on a miss you pay the cost of recomputing attention keys/values and also cold memory access which can add 100-200ms depending on model size and whether GPU kernel needs to reload chunks.
[02:58] Sam: can you unpack that  'KV cache miss' meaning what exactly in Redwood's runtime?
[03:02] Maya: sure, so Redwood maintains an in-memory KV cache for recent session prefixes. when the same session continues we reuse the KV cache on the same host, avoiding recomputation. misses happen if the request lands on a different host (routing imbalance), if the cache has been evicted due to memory pressure, or if you switch model variants (different kv key form).
[03:18] Jordan: also worth calling out cross-host routing  if you route across AZs or peered networks you add serialization/deserialization times and potential network spikes.
[03:27] Alex: our setup routes requests through our VPC with peering to Redwood, we have NAT gateway in the path which may add latency.
[03:33] Maya: NAT + egress + security inspection can add tens to hundreds ms unpredictably. For strict SLOs customers often choose dedicated capacity or private deployment to reduce network variability.
[03:43] Sam: ok what about batching  we've toyed with increasing batch window to improve throughput but worried about tail.
[03:50] Maya: batching is a tradeoff: larger batch windows improve throughput and amortize kernel startup, but they add queuing latency. For p95 you can often tune a small batch size to keep latency low; for p99 you need aggressive timeouts or prioritization for small requests. Redwood supports dynamic batching with latency targets  the runtime will flush after a configurable wall time or token count.
[04:12] Lina: do you have numbers? like batch size 8 vs 32 impact on p99?
[04:15] Maya: rough numbers depend on model and GPU  for a 13B dense model on A100-ish, batch 1 p95 ~120ms p99 ~420ms; batch 8 p95 ~95ms p99 ~500-700ms because some requests are queued in the tail. batch 32 improves throughput but increases median and tail. quantization can reduce compute time but may slightly increase variability if kernels are less mature.
[04:42] Alex: interesting, our med is fine but those p99 tails are killing the perceived latency. Is there a way to isolate the causes between network and compute?
[04:50] Maya: yes  controlled A/B: run the same traffic against a dedicated host in the same AZ vs hosted cross-AZ, and capture per-hop timing: LB->edge->host, TLS handshake, kv lookup, model forward. We also instrumented kernel-level timings and gProfiler traces. We'll share the benchmark spreadsheet with per-segment breakdown.
[05:08] Sam: what about streaming vs non-streaming measurement  how do you compare apples to apples?
[05:13] Maya: good point  measure time-to-first-token (TTFT) for streaming and time-to-complete for non-streaming. For UI interactivity TTFT matters more. For batch jobs total latency matters.
[05:24] Jordan: also consider client-side retries  if the client times out and re-sends that can amplify tail. you saw a trace earlier with a retry that doubled the apparent tail.
[05:33] Alex: we do have a 250ms client timeout for some endpoints causing retries on borderline p95s. maybe we should bump it.
[05:38] Maya: yes or implement idempotency keys + dedup at server so retries don't amplify load.
[05:44] Lina: we wanted to try quantized model variants  does Redwood support int8/e8-based profiles for dedicated?
[05:50] Maya: yes Redwood has quantization profiles, and the runtime will pick kernels accordingly. quantization reduces compute latency and memory pressure, often improving p95 and p99, but we recommend running evals because it can alter output distribution. For some workloads we saw p99 go from 420ms to 210ms after switching to an optimized int8 profile on dedicated nodes.
[06:10] Sam: caveat  if quantized kernels aren't hot in cache they may need extra kernel initializations?
[06:14] Maya: right sometimes first runs pay a small setup cost; warmup helps. Also if you mix quantized and non-quantized variants on the same host you can get eviction pressure.
[06:23] Jordan: operational knobs  pinned routing to avoid cross-host cache misses, keep-alive pools, connection reuse, smaller batch windows for latency-sensitive routes, and separate routes for streaming vs batch.
[06:33] Alex: what's the recommended approach for us given our traffic pattern  mostly low-latency chat bursts with occasional long responses?
[06:40] Maya: recommendation: 1) enable streaming for chat UI to improve TTFT, 2) set small batch target for that route (batch size 1-4, wall time 8-12ms), 3) pin sessions to hosts (sticky routing) for hot KV cache reuse, 4) consider dedicated capacity for worst-case SLOs or at minimum colocate in same AZ and avoid NAT paths, 5) try quantized profile in a canary.
[07:02] Sam: ok for the pinning  does that impact autoscaling or lead to imbalance?
[07:07] Maya: it can, so you should use session stickiness with a fallback policy; Redwood has autoscaling aware stickiness to avoid starvation. If traffic spikes we do fallback routing to nearest capacity which may cause misses, but you can configure overflow to a cheaper model variant.
[07:22] Lina: any notes about SOC2/compliance  we need audit logs for inference access in private mode?
[07:27] Jordan: yes private deployments include audit logs, KMS integration for keys, and optional on-prem package. Hosted includes logs too but for many enterprises private gives you full network control.
[07:36] Alex: ok let's talk next steps  we want that benchmark sheet, and we want Redwood to run a dedicated canary with quantized 13B and pinning to see impact on p99.
[07:46] Maya: we'll do that, I'll share the sheet and suggested bench config (traffic replay, TTFT and TTFComplete metrics, per-segment timings).
[07:54] Sam: we'll produce the representative replay corpus and check our client timeouts.
[07:59] Jordan: awesome  we'll aim to have preliminary numbers back within a week. thanks everyone.
[08:05] Alex: thanks all.
